OldNewChangeSource
1removedimport HL.SFLCompat
2removed
3removed-- # Typeclasses
4removed
5removed-- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**,
6removed-- declaring a type variable with no constraint on it:
7removed
8removedvariable (α : Type)
9removed
10removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
11removed-- Students will run across universes, though. When looking
12removed-- at List lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
13removed--
14removed-- `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
15removed--
16removed-- Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly
17removed-- ?
18removed
19removed-- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing
20removed-- functions like `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs
21removed-- like `List.length_reverse`, which use only the list's
22removed-- structure and never inspect any particular `a : α`.
23removed
24removed-- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving
25removed-- `α` completely generic, we want to partially specify its
26removed-- behavior. In Lean, this is done through a form of "ad hoc
27removed-- polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept originated
28removed-- in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from
29removed-- other languages, such as traits in Rust.
30removed
31removed-- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
32removed
33removed-- Consider the following function, which checks whether a
34removed-- natural number occurs in a list:
35removed
36removeddef List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
37removed match xs with
38removed | [] => false
39removed | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
40removed
41removedtheorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
42removed
43removedtheorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
44removed (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
45removed
46removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
47removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
48removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
49removed
50removed-- What if we want this to work for lists of **any** element
51removed-- type, not just `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests
52removed-- simply replacing `Nat` with a type variable `α`, but that
53removed-- produces a puzzling error:
54removed
55removed-- Note to developers:
56removed-- @dsainati - The Verso compilation is not actually
57removed-- removing this from the generated file despite th e -keep
58removed-- flag. It is, however, stripping the message guard, so
59removed-- this results in an error. Once we figure out how we are
60removed-- handling these cases, uncomment this.
61removed--
62removed-- `/--
63removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
64removed-- BEq α
65removed--
66removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
67removed-- -/
68removed-- #guard_msgs in
69removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
70removed-- match xs with
71removed-- | [] => false
72removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
73removed--
74removed-- `/--
75removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
76removed-- BEq α
77removed--
78removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
79removed-- -/
80removed-- #guard_msgs in
81removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
82removed-- match xs with
83removed-- | [] => false
84removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
85removed--
86removed-- `/--
87removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
88removed-- BEq α
89removed--
90removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
91removed-- -/
92removed-- #guard_msgs in
93removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
94removed-- match xs with
95removed-- | [] => false
96removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
97removed
98removed-- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==`
99removed-- should behave on a value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why
100removed-- shortly; for now, here's one way to sidestep the problem:
101removed-- have the caller supply the equality test to use.
102removed
103removedsf_experiment
104removed def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
105removed match xs with
106removed | [] => false
107removed | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
108removed
109removed #eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
110removed
111removed-- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and
112removed-- remember to supply, the right equality function.
113removed
114removed-- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer
115removed-- passing the function explicitly, Lean searches for one and
116removed-- provides it on its own. We specify something we want Lean to
117removed-- search for by declaring a `class` with the needed function
118removed-- as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a
119removed-- trait in Rust. Particular *implementations* of that
120removed-- interface, different ones for different types, are called
121removed-- *instances*. Finally, we add the name of that class as a
122removed-- *typeclass constraint* on the polymorphic variable that the
123removed-- function applies to. This directs Lean to use the interface
124removed-- inside the function, and to find and fill in the appropriate
125removed-- instance at call-sites to that function. Here is what this
126removed-- looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
127removed
128removeddef List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
129removed match xs with
130removed | [] => false
131removed | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
132removed
133removedtheorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
134removed
135removedtheorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
136removed (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
137removed
138removed#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
139removed
140removed-- As Lists noted when we first used it, `==` on `Nat` comes
141removed-- from the `BEq` typeclass, and it's what `List.elem_poly`
142removed-- uses internally wherever it writes `==`. This is done using
143removed-- **instance implicits**, where we place a desired typeclass
144removed-- assumption in square bracket. The `[BEq α]` constraint is
145removed-- saying that an instance of `BEq` must be provided at call
146removed-- sites for the *particular* type `α` that is used. In the
147removed-- example `[0, 1].elem_poly 0`, this type is `Nat`, and the
148removed-- automatically chosen instance corresponds to `Nat.beq`.
149removed
150removed-- Note to developers (xhalo32):
151removed-- This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`,
152removed-- which comes from `DecidableEq`, does not contain
153removed-- `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of `List.elem_nat`
154removed-- versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
155removed-- how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
156removed
157removed-- In the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, `α` was fully
158removed-- generic, with no typeclass constraint — so the `==` in its
159removed-- body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and no
160removed-- single `BEq` instance can do that. That's why Lean's search
161removed-- failed.
162removed
163removed-- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen
164removed-- so far. We'll see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in
165removed-- below, starting with how to define a typeclass in the first
166removed-- place.
167removed
168removed-- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
169removed
170removed-- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a
171removed-- typeclass of our own, to see the mechanism — classes,
172removed-- instances, and synthesis — that made `==` resolve
173removed-- automatically above.
174removed
175removed-- Suppose we want to specify that a type has at least one
176removed-- inhabitant, i.e., that it is not empty. A `structure`
177removed-- (chapter Lists) can express this directly:
178removed
179removedstructure HasOneStruct (α : Type) where
180removed one : α
181removed
182removed-- A value of `HasOneStruct Nat` witnesses that `Nat` is
183removed-- inhabited: it's built the same way any structure is, by
184removed-- supplying a `Nat` for the `one` field:
185removed
186removeddef nat_hasOneStruct : HasOneStruct Nat where
187removed one := 1
188removed
189removedexample : nat_hasOneStruct.one = 1 := rfl
190removed
191removed-- But nothing makes Lean produce this witness
192removed-- **automatically**: we had to write `⟨1⟩` ourselves, unlike
193removed-- the `BEq Nat` instance that Lean found for us on its own
194removed-- above.
195removed
196removed-- Typeclasses solve this. In Lean, they're implemented as
197removed-- structures and declared the same way, but with `class` in
198removed-- place of `structure`:
199removed
200removedclass HasOne (α : Type) where
201removed one : α
202removed
203removed-- The difference is in how we provide values of this type.
204removed-- Instead of `def`, we use `instance`:
205removed
206removed-- Note to developers:
207removed-- From GitHub (@chenson2018): Part of the point here is
208removed-- that we don't usually refer to instances explicitly,
209removed-- even me providing an explicit name is for pedagogy
210removed-- reasons. I'll make it more explicit in the text that
211removed-- what we're looking for in the infoview is the presence
212removed-- of this instance.
213removed
214removedinstance instHasOneNat : HasOne Nat where
215removed one := 1
216removed
217removed-- Lean can now find this instance on its own, via **typeclass
218removed-- synthesis** (or **typeclass inference**) — the same process
219removed-- that found `BEq Nat` earlier. To see it choose between
220removed-- instances, declare a second one, for `Int`, the type of
221removed-- integers `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
222removed
223removedinstance instHasOneInt : HasOne Int where
224removed one := -1
225removed
226removed-- Now `HasOne.one` alone, with no instance named, is enough —
227removed-- Lean infers which instance we mean from the expected type:
228removed
229removedexample : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
230removedexample : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
231removed
232removed-- These are the same as naming the instances explicitly:
233removed
234removedexample : instHasOneNat.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
235removedexample : instHasOneInt.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
236removed
237removed-- The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
238removed
239removedset_option pp.all true in
240removedexample : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
241removed
242removedset_option pp.all true in
243removedexample : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
244removed
245removed-- which reveals `@HasOne.one Nat instHasOneNat` and
246removed-- `@HasOne.one Int instHasOneInt` on the right-hand side of
247removed-- each equality. The `#synth` command runs the same search
248removed-- directly:
249removed
250removed#synth HasOne Nat
251removed
252removed-- instHasOneNat
253removed
254removed-- For a typeclass like `HasOne` that carries data — a term,
255removed-- such as the `1` above, rather than only proofs — we expect
256removed-- at most one instance per type, so this search has a unique
257removed-- answer.
258removed
259removed-- Note to developers:
260removed-- @chenson2018: I don't really want to explain diamonds
261removed-- here, is the above white lie hand-waving okay??
262removed
263removed-- We'll put `HasOne`'s standard-library cousin, `Inhabited`,
264removed-- to work later in this chapter, when maps need a default
265removed-- value for a generic type. First, though, let's go back to
266removed-- `List.elem_poly` and see how its `[BEq α]` argument actually
267removed-- gets resolved.
268removed
269removed-- ## Using Typeclasses
270removed
271removed-- Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with
272removed-- notation display turned off:
273removed
274removedset_option pp.notation false in
275removed#check 1 == 2
276removed
277removed-- Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for
278removed-- `BEq.beq`, a field of exactly the kind of typeclass we just
279removed-- learned to define:
280removed
281removed-- class BEq (α : Type u) where
282removed-- /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
283removed-- beq : α → α → Bool
284removed
285removed-- Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of
286removed-- `BEq` for the type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched
287removed-- for a `HasOne` instance above. For `Nat`, that instance is:
288removed
289removedinstance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
290removed beq := Nat.beq
291removed
292removed-- This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when
293removed-- `List.elem_poly` is called on a `List Nat` — no different
294removed-- from Lean choosing `instHasOneNat` for `HasOne.one` earlier.
295removed
296removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
297removed
298removed-- Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when
299removed-- specialized to natural numbers.
300removed
301removedtheorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
302removed sorry
303removed
304removed-- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
305removed
306removed-- Notably, the above examples enforce no conditions on the
307removed-- data that they carry, and we could provide any value that we
308removed-- would like for `HasOne.one`. This could be misleading, for
309removed-- instance if we had instead defined an instance
310removed
311removedsf_experiment
312removed instance : HasOne Nat where
313removed one := 2
314removed
315removed-- we might have some counterintuitive proofs based on the name
316removed-- leading us to believe the class contained the element `1`.
317removed-- In most languages that support typeclasses it is not
318removed-- possible to enforce a notion of "lawfulness" as part of the
319removed-- typeclass, and it falls to the author to ensure that any
320removed-- desired invariants are satisfied.
321removed
322removed-- As an example, suppose that we wanted to express the idea
323removed-- that a type has at least two distinct elements. A first
324removed-- attempt might be
325removed
326removedsf_experiment
327removed class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
328removed one : α
329removed two : α
330removed
331removed-- but this does not disallow the case where `one` and `two`
332removed-- are equal. In a proof assistant, however, typeclasses can
333removed-- also carry proofs along with data, so we can write
334removed
335removedclass HasTwo (α : Type) where
336removed one : α
337removed two : α
338removed one_neq_two : one ≠ two
339removed
340removed-- to enforce that these are two distinct entries. Declaring
341removed-- instances works in much the same way as before, except that
342removed-- now `HasTwo.one_neq_two` requires a proof:
343removed
344removedinstance : HasTwo Nat where
345removed one := 1
346removed two := 2
347removed one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
348removed
349removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
350removed
351removed-- Following the pattern of `HasOne` and `HasTwo`, define a
352removed-- class `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three
353removed-- distinct elements.
354removed
355removed-- Note to developers (Claude, NOW):
356removed-- Rendering bug in this exercise and `instHasThree` below.
357removed-- Both use the `-- SOLUTION`/`-- END SOLUTION`
358removed-- comment-marker idiom to hide **some** class fields /
359removed-- instance fields, but the Verso HTML build does not
360removed-- process those markers (only the `solution!` tactic is
361removed-- handled). In **student** and **terse** the class shows
362removed-- only the visible fields while the `instHasThree`
363removed-- instance then reports a spurious
364removed-- `Fields missing: one_neq_three, two_neq_three` error; in
365removed-- **solutions** the hidden fields are shown but the
366removed-- literal `-- SOLUTION` / `-- END SOLUTION` comment lines
367removed-- leak into the displayed code. The generated `.lean` is
368removed-- fine — HTML-only. Fix by expressing the hidden fields
369removed-- with `solution!` rather than the comment markers.
370removed
371removedclass HasThree (α : Type) where
372removed one : α
373removed two : α
374removed three : α
375removed one_neq_two : one ≠ two
376removed -- FILL IN HERE
377removed
378removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): instHasThree ⭐
379removed
380removed-- Provide an instance of `HasThree` for `Nat`.
381removed
382removedinstance : HasThree Nat where
383removed one := 1
384removed two := 2
385removed three := 3
386removed one_neq_two := sorry
387removed -- FILL IN HERE
388removed
389removed-- ## Maps
390removed
391removed-- Maps (or dictionaries) are ubiquitous data structures both
392removed-- in ordinary programming and in the theory of programming
393removed-- languages; we're going to need them in many places in the
394removed-- coming chapters.
395removed
396removed-- We'll define two flavors of maps: total maps, which include
397removed-- a "default" element to be returned when a key being looked
398removed-- up doesn't exist, and partial maps, which instead return an
399removed-- option to indicate success or failure. Partial maps are
400removed-- defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as the default
401removed-- element.
402removed
403removed-- ### Identifiers
404removed
405removed-- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we
406removed-- will use to index into our maps. Instead of using concrete
407removed-- types, we will use a type variables
408removed
409removedvariable {α : Type} {β : Type} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] [LawfulBEq α]
410removed
411removedset_option linter.unusedSectionVars false
412removed
413removed-- where `α` is the type of our map keys and `β` the
414removed-- corresponding values. Looking at `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq`,
415removed-- we see that these typeclasses:
416removed
417removed-- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
418removed-- class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
419removed-- /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
420removed-- protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
421removed
422removed-- /--
423removed-- A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
424removed
425removed-- In other words:
426removed-- * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
427removed-- * `a == a` is true.
428removed-- -/
429removed-- class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
430removed-- /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
431removed-- eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
432removed
433removed-- provide the assumption that we have an boolean equality
434removed-- (`==`) on our keys that is reflexive and coincides with
435removed-- proposition equality `=`.
436removed
437removed-- ### Total Maps
438removed
439removed-- Our main job in this chapter will be to build a definition
440removed-- of partial maps that is similar in behavior to the one we
441removed-- saw in the Lists chapter, plus accompanying lemmas about its
442removed-- behavior.
443removed
444removed-- This time around, though, we're going to use functions,
445removed-- rather than lists of key-value pairs, to build maps. The
446removed-- advantage of this representation is that it offers a more
447removed-- "extensional" view of maps: two maps that respond to queries
448removed-- in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
449removed-- function, rather than just as "equivalent" list structures.
450removed-- This simplifies proofs that use maps.
451removed
452removed-- We build up to partial maps in two steps. First, we define
453removed-- total maps that return a default value when we look up a key
454removed-- that is not present in the map.
455removed
456removeddef TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) := α → β
457removed
458removednamespace TotalMap
459removed
460removed-- Intuitively, a total map over an element type `β` is just a
461removed-- function that can be looked up using a corresponding
462removed-- `a : α`.
463removed
464removed-- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the
465removed-- `Inhabited` typeclass, which is the standard library's
466removed-- implementation of our `HasOne` example from above:
467removed
468removedvariable [Inhabited β]
469removed
470removed-- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map,
471removed-- given a default element; this map always returns the default
472removed-- element when applied to any string.
473removed
474removeddef empty : TotalMap α β := fun _ ↦ default
475removed
476removed-- and we'll also declare an instance
477removed
478removedinstance : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
479removed emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
480removed
481removed-- so that we can use the `∅` notation for this empty map.
482removed
483removed-- #### Getting Elements
484removed
485removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
486removed-- This introductory bit seems heavier than necessary. Why
487removed-- not just say that we want to treat TotalMap as an
488removed-- abstract thing, not rely on the fact that it is defined
489removed-- in terms of functions, and then go ahead and do that?
490removed
491removed-- To access values in a map (i.e., a function), we can apply
492removed-- the map to a key:
493removed
494removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson (chenson2018), Niklas Halonen (xhalo32)):
495removed-- Using `default` in the early examples might be
496removed-- confusing. We could use something concrete, like `0`
497removed-- which is the default `Nat` instead.
498removed
499removedexample : (∅ : TotalMap Nat Nat) 1 = default := rfl
500removed
501removedend TotalMap
502removed
503removed-- Here we have made use of the the fact that the type
504removed-- `TotalMap` is defined as a function type, so technically
505removed-- Lean lets us use a function application to get an element.
506removed-- While this is possible, it goes against the spirit we have
507removed-- seen in previous chapters of defining interfaces to our
508removed-- types, like characterizing lemmas. We would like that the
509removed-- public interface we design for TotalMap to be independent of
510removed-- the fact that the definition is `α → β`.
511removed
512removed-- In the ideal, we should be able to substitute a different
513removed-- type with similar behavior without needing to change the
514removed-- public interface. Suppose, just for the sake of argument,
515removed-- that we wanted to define total maps as `List (α × β)` or
516removed-- `Std.HashMap α β`. Neither of these are functions, so the
517removed-- syntax `∅ 1` wouldn't work. If this is the public interface
518removed-- to access elements, it restricts the definition ot
519removed-- `TotalMap`, forcing it to be a function of some kind.
520removed
521removed-- To abstract away the function application, we introduce
522removed-- notation for accessing elements using square brackets. This
523removed-- let's us write `∅[1]` or `m[a]` regardless of the underlying
524removed-- definition of `TotalMap`.
525removed
526removed-- We'll call the typeclass `MyGetElem`. The typeclass takes
527removed-- three type parameters: the collection, the keys that can be
528removed-- used to index and the elements that it returns. For example,
529removed-- let's say we have declared an instance
530removed-- `MyGetElem (List Bool) Nat Bool`. One can think of the
531removed-- instance as saying that *indexing into `xs : List Bool` with
532removed-- an index `i : Nat` returns a `Bool`*. The notation we
533removed-- introduce for this is: `xs[i] = MyGetElem.getElem xs i`.
534removed
535removed-- Don't worry about what `outParam Type` means (it's like a
536removed-- normal type parameter with a hint to Lean that helps
537removed-- typeclass inference). The `macro_rules` and the
538removed-- `app_unexpander` are minor technicalities for getting the
539removed-- syntax to work.
540removed
541removedclass MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
542removed getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
543removed
544removednamespace MyGetElem
545removedscoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => `(getElem $xs $i)
546removed
547removed@[app_unexpander getElem]
548removeddef unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
549removed | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
550removed | _ => throw ()
551removedend MyGetElem
552removed
553removedopen scoped MyGetElem
554removed
555removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
556removed-- Make sure we've really explained `open scoped`
557removed-- somewhere...
558removed
559removed-- To use the notation `m[a]` to access elements of a map `m`,
560removed-- we add a `MyGetElem` instance for total maps.
561removed
562removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
563removed-- Have we explained `variable [Inhabited β]`?
564removed
565removednamespace TotalMap
566removedvariable [Inhabited β]
567removed
568removedinstance : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
569removed getElem m a := m a
570removed
571removedtheorem getElem_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m a := by rfl
572removed
573removedexample : (∅ : TotalMap Nat Nat)[1] = default := by rfl
574removed
575removed-- When proving some of the characterizing lemmas below, we
576removed-- will rewrite using `getElem_def`. However, `getElem_def`
577removed-- exposes the underlying implementation that accessing
578removed-- elements in total maps is a function application, therefore
579removed-- it should only be used sparingly, and only inside the
580removed-- `TotalMap` namespace.
581removed
582removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
583removed-- That is a bit mysterious.
584removed
585removed-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
586removed-- As per the discussion in
587removed-- `https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean/pull/166#discussion_r3690573597`,
588removed-- we should provide the reverse of `getElem_def` as a
589removed-- simp-lemma, but it doesn't seem to behave nicely:
590removed--
591removed-- `@[simp]
592removed-- theorem apply_eq_getElem (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m a = m[a] := by rfl`
593removed--
594removed-- The reverse direction of `getElem_def` is provided as a
595removed-- `simp`-lemma.
596removed--
597removed-- `example (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m a = m[a] := by
598removed-- -- simp -- doesn't work (infinite loop)
599removed-- -- dsimp -- doesn't work (nothing happens)
600removed-- -- rw [apply_eq_getElem] -- doesn't work: The pattern to be substituted is a metavariable (`?m ?a`) in this equality: ?m ?a = ?m[?a]
601removed-- rw [apply_eq_getElem m a] -- works`
602removed--
603removed-- Explanation of the infinite loop by Yipeng Liu
604removed-- (berberman): To see why, with
605removed-- `trace.Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite` enabled and specifying
606removed-- maxSteps to simp, we can track what's going on:
607removed--
608removed-- `[Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
609removed-- m a
610removed-- ==>
611removed-- m[a]
612removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
613removed-- m[a]
614removed-- ==>
615removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
616removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
617removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
618removed-- ==>
619removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
620removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
621removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
622removed-- ==>
623removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
624removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
625removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
626removed-- ==>...`
627removed--
628removed-- So I think the issue here is that the LHS m a is too
629removed-- board, causing this lemma repeating itself. First we
630removed-- have `m a => m[a], but m[a]` is defeq to
631removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem m) a, and nevertheless we require m
632removed-- to be a TotalMap, a TotalMap is defeq to α → β. So this
633removed-- lemma applies again --
634removed-- `(MyGetElem.getElem m) a => (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]`
635removed-- which is `(MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]`
636removed-- and keep going.
637removed
638removed-- #### Updating
639removed
640removed-- More interesting is the map-updating function, which (as
641removed-- always) takes a map `m`, a key `a`, and a value `b` and
642removed-- returns a new map that takes `a` to `b` and takes every
643removed-- other key to whatever `m` does. The novelty here is that we
644removed-- achieve this effect by wrapping a new function around the
645removed-- old one.
646removed
647removeddef update (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β :=
648removed fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
649removed
650removed-- This definition is a nice example of higher-order
651removed-- programming: `update` takes a function `m` and yields a new
652removed-- function `fun x' ↦ ...` that behaves like the desired map.
653removed
654removed-- For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`,
655removed-- where `"foo"` and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every
656removed-- other key is mapped to `false`, like this:
657removed
658removeddef exampleMap :=
659removed (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
660removed |>.update "foo" true
661removed |>.update "bar" true
662removed
663removed-- We'll also introduce a notation for updating maps
664removed
665removednotation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
666removed
667removedtheorem update_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
668removed a →ₜ b ; m = fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := rfl
669removed
670removed-- We can also hide the last case when it is empty:
671removed
672removednotation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
673removed
674removed-- The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
675removed
676removeddef exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
677removeddef exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
678removed
679removed-- This completes the definition of total maps.
680removed
681removedexample : exampleMap = exampleMap' := rfl
682removedexample : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := rfl
683removed
684removedexample : exampleMap'["baz"] = false := rfl
685removedexample : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := rfl
686removedexample : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := rfl
687removedexample : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := rfl
688removed
689removed-- When we use maps in later chapters, we'll need several
690removed-- fundamental facts about how they behave.
691removed
692removed-- Even if you don't work the following exercises, make sure
693removed-- you thoroughly understand the statements of the lemmas!
694removed
695removed-- (Some of the proofs require the functional extensionality
696removed-- axiom, which was discussed in the Logic chapter.)
697removed
698removed-- First, the empty map returns its default element for all
699removed-- keys:
700removed
701removedtheorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : TotalMap α β)[a] = default := rfl
702removed
703removed-- Next, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a new value
704removed-- `b` and then look up `a` in the map resulting from the
705removed-- `update`, we get back `b`:
706removed
707removedtheorem update_eq (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₜ b ; m)[a] = b := by
708removed rw [update_def, getElem_def, ReflBEq.rfl, cond_true]
709removed
710removed-- On the other hand, if we update a map `m` at a key `a₁` and
711removed-- then look up a *different* key `a₂` in the resulting map, we
712removed-- get the same result that `m` would have given:
713removed
714removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_neq ⭐⭐
715removed
716removedtheorem update_neq {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
717removed (a₁ →ₜ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
718removed sorry
719removed
720removed-- The two remaining facts are equalities *between maps*, so we
721removed-- first need to say when two maps are equal. Since a total map
722removed-- *is* a function, this is exactly the functional
723removed-- extensionality principle from the Logic chapter: two maps
724removed-- are equal when they agree at every key. Recording it once,
725removed-- for maps, and tagging it `@[ext]` lets the `ext` tactic
726removed-- reduce a goal `m₁ = m₂` to the pointwise one in the proofs
727removed-- below.
728removed
729removed@[ext]
730removedtheorem ext {m₁ m₂ : TotalMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := funext h
731removed
732removed-- If we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a value `b₁` and
733removed-- then update again with the same key `a` and another value
734removed-- `b₂`, the resulting map behaves the same (gives the same
735removed-- result when applied to any key) as the simpler map obtained
736removed-- by performing just the second `update` on `m`:
737removed
738removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_shadow ⭐⭐
739removed
740removedtheorem update_shadow (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b₁ b₂ : β) :
741removed (a →ₜ b₂ ; a →ₜ b₁ ; m) = (a →ₜ b₂ ; m) := by
742removed sorry
743removed
744removed-- Given keys `a₁` and `a₂`, the tactic `by_cases`
745removed-- `h : a₁ = a₂` splits the proof into the case where they are
746removed-- equal — where `subst h` then replaces one by the other — and
747removed-- the case where they are not, which is what `update_neq`
748removed-- wants. Use it to prove the following theorem, which states
749removed-- that if we update a map to assign key `a` the same value as
750removed-- it already has in `m`, then the result is equal to `m`:
751removed
752removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1, NOW):
753removed-- Two things the Rocq source says here have been dropped.
754removed--
755removed-- Rocq frames this case analysis around
756removed-- `destruct (eqb_spec x1 x2)`, which "simultaneously
757removed-- performs case analysis on the result of
758removed-- `String.eqb x1 x2` and generates hypotheses about the
759removed-- equality (in the sense of `=`) of `x1` and `x2`" — the
760removed-- boolean/propositional reflection idiom. The paragraph
761removed-- above replaces that with `by_cases`/`subst`, which is
762removed-- what the Lean proof uses. But reflection is what the
763removed-- `Reflection` section **below** is about, so the two may
764removed-- want to be connected rather than have one silently
765removed-- displace the other.
766removed--
767removed-- Rocq then says "With the example in chapter **IndProp**
768removed-- as a template, use `String.eqb_spec` to prove ...". That
769removed-- cross-reference is dropped, since it is unclear what the
770removed-- Lean `IndProp` chapter will end up containing. Revisit
771removed-- later.
772removed
773removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_same ⭐⭐
774removed
775removedtheorem update_same (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : (a →ₜ m[a] ; m) = m := by
776removed sorry
777removed
778removed-- Similarly, prove one final property of the `update`
779removed-- function: if we update a map `m` at two distinct keys, it
780removed-- doesn't matter in which order we do the updates.
781removed
782removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1, NOW):
783removed-- Rocq says "Similarly, use `String.eqb_spec` to prove
784removed-- ..."; the instruction to use a specific lemma is dropped
785removed-- here for the same reason as in the note above.
786removed
787removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): update_permute ⭐⭐⭐
788removed
789removedtheorem update_permute {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} {b₁ b₂ : β} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) :
790removed (a₁ →ₜ b₁ ; a₂ →ₜ b₂ ; m) = (a₂ →ₜ b₂ ; a₁ →ₜ b₁ ; m) := by
791removed sorry
792removed
793removed-- Note to developers:
794removed-- The Rocq source also has `getElem_empty` (originally
795removed-- `apply_empty`) and `update_eq` as (optional) exercises;
796removed-- here they are worked examples, since `update_eq` was
797removed-- already presented that way. Reconsider if this section
798removed-- is rebalanced.
799removed
800removedend TotalMap
801removed
802removed-- ### Notation for Concrete Maps
803removed
804removed-- Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural notation
805removed-- for concrete maps like `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To
806removed-- accomplish this we define a simple structure that consists
807removed-- of a key and a value along with `↦` notation for it.
808removed
809removed/--
810removedA key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
811removed-/
812removed@[ext]
813removedstructure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
814removed key : K
815removed value : V
816removed
817removednamespace KVPair
818removedscoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
819removedend KVPair
820removed
821removedopen scoped KVPair
822removed
823removed-- Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances which
824removed-- control the `{}` notation in lean.
825removed
826removednamespace TotalMap
827removed
828removedvariable [Inhabited β]
829removed
830removedinstance : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
831removed insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
832removed
833removedinstance : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
834removed singleton kv := insert kv ∅
835removed
836removedinstance : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
837removed insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
838removed
839removedend TotalMap
840removed
841removed-- Here are a couple of examples using the new notation:
842removed
843removedexample : ({ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }) = "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅ := rfl
844removed
845removedexample : ({ "foo" ↦ true } : TotalMap String Bool)["foo"] = true := rfl
846removed
847removedexample : ({ 1 ↦ 2, 1 ↦ 3 } : TotalMap Nat Nat)[1] = 2 := rfl
848removed
849removed-- The reason we need to explicitly specify the type of the map
850removed-- is that Lean doesn't know what type of collection
851removed-- `{ "foo" ↦ true }` is without type hints, as we can see with
852removed-- `#check`:
853removed
854removed#check { "foo" ↦ true }
855removed
856removed-- {"foo" ↦ true} : ?m.4
857removed
858removed-- The type shows a `?m.4`, which indicates that Lean can't
859removed-- infer the type. A type which can't be inferred doesn't have
860removed-- any type classes like `MyGetElem`, so typeclass resolution
861removed-- gets stuck in the following example:
862removed
863removedsf_expect_failure
864removed example : ({ "foo" ↦ true })["foo"] = true := rfl
865removed
866removed-- ### Partial Maps
867removed
868removed-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
869removed-- We should spend some time discussing differences between
870removed-- the inductive approach in Lists.lean and the approach
871removed-- here. The inductive approach could be made polymorphic
872removed-- and proven to be equivalent with partial maps (I
873removed-- believe), so the point is not that the maps are
874removed-- extensionally different. A question (that I don't have
875removed-- an answer to) is then: what makes the new partial map
876removed-- better?
877removed
878removed-- Lastly, we define *partial maps* on top of total maps. A
879removed-- partial map with elements of type `β` is simply a total map
880removed-- with elements of type `Option β`, whose default element is
881removed-- `none`.
882removed
883removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
884removed-- I don't understand the comment on the `inner` field...
885removed--
886removed-- Niklas Halonen (xhalo32): This is just a technical note
887removed-- that discourages using `PartialMap.inner` over
888removed-- `PartialMap.toTotal`. We don't want both to appear in
889removed-- the public API. Compare with `MeasurableSet'` in
890removed-- https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/1f8806b67d6f09e6d2552c031e6d3a3171016116/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/MeasurableSpace/Defs.lean#L52
891removed-- which doesn't appear in the public API (it uses
892removed-- `MeasurableSet` instead).
893removed
894removedstructure PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
895removed /-- The inner total map. Should not appear in the public API, use `PartialMap.toTotal` instead. -/
896removed inner : TotalMap α (Option β)
897removed
898removedinstance : EmptyCollection (PartialMap α β) where
899removed emptyCollection := { inner := ∅ }
900removed
901removeddef PartialMap.toTotal (m : PartialMap α β) : TotalMap α (Option β) := m.inner
902removed
903removedinstance : MyGetElem (PartialMap α β) α (Option β) where
904removed getElem m a := m.toTotal[a]
905removed
906removedtheorem getElem_def (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.toTotal[a] := rfl
907removed
908removed-- Remember that we discussed earlier with total maps that
909removed-- using function application exposes the implementation, and
910removed-- that's why we introduced a new notation `MyGetElem`? Here we
911removed-- take that concept to a new level, and instead of using a
912removed-- `def` for partial maps, like this...
913removed
914removed-- def PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) := TotalMap α (Option β)`
915removed
916removed-- ...we define partial maps as a structure containing just a
917removed-- total map. This more strongly hides the fact that it's a
918removed-- total map.
919removed
920removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
921removed-- If this way is better, then why didn't we do it for
922removed-- total maps too? Just for the sake of explaining two
923removed-- different mechanisms? We should explain our reasoning.
924removed
925removed-- Now, the type system doesn't consider `PartialMap α β` to be
926removed-- definitionally equal to `TotalMap α (Option β)`, so the
927removed-- following equality doesn't type check:
928removed
929removedsf_expect_failure
930removed example : (∅ : PartialMap α β) = (∅ : TotalMap α (Option β)) := by rfl
931removed
932removed-- Type mismatch
933removed-- ∅
934removed-- has type
935removed-- TotalMap α (Option β)
936removed-- but is expected to have type
937removed-- PartialMap α β
938removed
939removed-- Note to developers (Claude, NOW):
940removed-- The Maps chapter removed the `optionCoe` instance for
941removed-- the duration of its partial-map development
942removed-- (`attribute [-instance] optionCoe`, restored at
943removed-- `end PartialMap`), on the grounds that a coercion from
944removed-- `β` to `Option β` might be confusing at this point. It
945removed-- also recorded two things about doing so: the removal
946removed-- must not leak to end-of-file, or Verso's `tag`/`file`
947removed-- metadata coercion (`Tag → Option Tag`) fails at
948removed-- end-of-document; and `[-instance]` cannot be scoped
949removed-- `local`, hence the manual add/restore pair.
950removed--
951removed-- We have not carried that over — nothing here needs it
952removed-- and it is not clear it is wanted. Decide whether to
953removed-- reinstate it.
954removed
955removed-- Updating a partial map at a key means storing a `some` value
956removed-- there. To update, we create a new partial map from
957removed-- `a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal` by wrapping it in angle brackets,
958removed-- i.e. using the anonymous constructor syntax. This is
959removed-- equivalent to writing
960removed-- `{ inner := a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal }`. We also introduce a
961removed-- similar notation for it as for total maps.
962removed
963removednamespace PartialMap
964removed
965removeddef update (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : PartialMap α β :=
966removed ⟨a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal⟩
967removed
968removednotation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => PartialMap.update m a b
969removed
970removednotation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 => PartialMap.update ∅ a b
971removed
972removeddef examplePmap : PartialMap String Bool := "Church" →ₚ true ; "Turing" →ₚ false
973removed
974removed-- Next, we provide some fundamental properties about
975removed-- `toTotal`:
976removed
977removedtheorem toTotal_empty : (∅ : PartialMap α β).toTotal = (∅ : TotalMap α (Option β)) := rfl
978removed
979removedtheorem toTotal_update (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
980removed (a →ₚ b ; m).toTotal = a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal := rfl
981removed
982removed-- As an example, here's how we can use these on some concrete
983removed-- maps:
984removed
985removedexample : (2 →ₚ 3)[2] = some 3 := by
986removed rw [getElem_def, toTotal_update, toTotal_empty, TotalMap.getElem_def]
987removed rfl
988removed
989removed-- This also holds by definition (`rfl`), since all the
990removed-- rewrites in the above proof do the computation step-by-step.
991removed
992removedexample : (2 →ₚ 3)[2] = some 3 := by rfl
993removed
994removed-- Next, we lift all of the basic lemmas about total maps to
995removed-- partial maps. To do this we should first prove an
996removed-- extensionality lemma about partial maps. To prove
997removed-- extensionality, we employ injectivity of `PartialMap`'s
998removed-- constructor `mk` using `mk.injEq`.
999removed
1000removedtheorem toTotal_eq_iff (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : m₁.toTotal = m₂.toTotal ↔ m₁ = m₂ := by
1001removed rw [mk.injEq]
1002removed rfl
1003removed
1004removed@[ext]
1005removedtheorem ext {m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := by
1006removed rw [← toTotal_eq_iff]
1007removed exact TotalMap.ext h
1008removed
1009removed-- Now, let's lift the `TotalMap` lemmas:
1010removed
1011removedtheorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : PartialMap α β)[a] = none := by
1012removed rw [getElem_def, toTotal_empty, TotalMap.getElem_empty, Option.default_eq_none]
1013removed
1014removedtheorem update_eq (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₚ b ; m)[a] = some b := by
1015removed rw [getElem_def, toTotal_update, TotalMap.update_eq]
1016removed
1017removedtheorem update_neq {m : PartialMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
1018removed (a₁ →ₚ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
1019removed dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
1020removed rw [TotalMap.update_neq h]
1021removed
1022removedtheorem update_shadow (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b₁ b₂ : β) :
1023removed (a →ₚ b₂ ; a →ₚ b₁ ; m) = (a →ₚ b₂ ; m) := by
1024removed apply ext
1025removed intro x
1026removed dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
1027removed rw [TotalMap.update_shadow]
1028removed
1029removedtheorem update_same {m : PartialMap α β} {a : α} {b : β} (h : m[a] = some b) :
1030removed (a →ₚ b ; m) = m := by
1031removed apply ext
1032removed intro x
1033removed dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
1034removed rw [← h, getElem_def, TotalMap.update_same]
1035removed
1036removedtheorem update_permute {m : PartialMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} {b₁ b₂ : β} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) :
1037removed (a₁ →ₚ b₁ ; a₂ →ₚ b₂ ; m) = (a₂ →ₚ b₂ ; a₁ →ₚ b₁ ; m) := by
1038removed apply ext
1039removed intro x
1040removed dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
1041removed rw [TotalMap.update_permute h]
1042removed
1043removed-- And let's add `{}`-notation for partial maps as well.
1044removed
1045removedinstance : Insert (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
1046removed insert kv m := kv.key →ₚ kv.value ; m
1047removed
1048removedinstance : Singleton (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
1049removed singleton kv := insert kv ∅
1050removed
1051removedinstance : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
1052removed insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
1053removed
1054removedexample : { 1 ↦ 2, 2 ↦ 3 } = 1 →ₚ 2 ; 2 →ₚ 3 := rfl
1055removed
1056removed-- One last thing: for partial maps, it's convenient to
1057removed-- introduce a notion of map inclusion, stating that all the
1058removed-- entries in one map are also present in another. Lean already
1059removed-- has notation for this — `m₁ ⊆ m₂` — which we get by
1060removed-- supplying a `HasSubset` instance.
1061removed
1062removed-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
1063removed-- I think it would be more idiomatic to define `Subset` as
1064removed-- `∀ {a : α} {b : β}, m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b`.
1065removed
1066removeddef Subset (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : Prop :=
1067removed ∀ (a : α) (b : β), m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b
1068removed
1069removedinstance : HasSubset (PartialMap α β) where
1070removed Subset := PartialMap.Subset
1071removed
1072removedtheorem subset_def (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) :
1073removed m₁ ⊆ m₂ ↔ (∀ (a : α) (b : β), m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b) := .rfl
1074removed
1075removed-- We can then show that map update preserves map inclusion,
1076removed-- that is:
1077removed
1078removedtheorem update_subset (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) (h : m₁ ⊆ m₂) :
1079removed (a →ₚ b ; m₁) ⊆ (a →ₚ b ; m₂) := by
1080removed rw [subset_def] at h ⊢
1081removed intro a' b' hb
1082removed by_cases ha : a = a'
1083removed · subst ha
1084removed rw [update_eq] at hb ⊢
1085removed exact hb
1086removed · rw [update_neq ha] at hb ⊢
1087removed exact h a' b' hb
1088removed
1089removedend PartialMap
1090removed
1091removed-- This property is quite useful for reasoning about languages
1092removed-- with variable binding — e.g., the Simply Typed Lambda
1093removed-- Calculus, which we will see in *Type Systems*, where maps
1094removed-- are used to keep track of which program variables are
1095removed-- defined in a given scope.
1096removed

1098removed-- `namespace TotalMap` is reopened here only because the

1105removednamespace TotalMap

1107removed-- ## Reflection
1108removed
1109removed-- Note to developers:
1110removed-- I think this will still exist in previous chapters, just
1111removed-- not have the reflection explanations until here? Since I
1112removed-- can't import these yet, just placing here at the top of

1114removed-- even as boolean computation and Prop should go below,
1115removed-- after the table where we explain the difference.
1116removed
1117removednamespace Nat
1118removed
1119removed@[irreducible]
1120removeddef isEven : Nat → Bool
1121removed| 0 => true
1122removed| 1 => false
1123removed| n + 2 => isEven n
1124removed
1125removed@[irreducible]
1126removeddef double : Nat → Nat
1127removed| 0 => 0
1128removed| n + 1 => double n + 2
1129removed
1130removedsection
1131removed
1132removedunseal isEven
1133removedunseal double
1134removed
1135removedtheorem isEven_zero : isEven 0 = true := rfl
1136removedtheorem isEven_one : isEven 1 = false := rfl
1137removedtheorem isEven_succ_succ (n : Nat) : isEven (n + 2) = isEven n := rfl
1138removed
1139removedtheorem double_zero : double 0 = 0 := by rfl
1140removedtheorem double_succ (n : Nat) : double (n + 1) = double n + 2 := rfl
1141removed
1142removedend
1143removed
1144removeddef Even (n : Nat) := ∃ m, n = double m
1145removed
1146removedtheorem isEven_succ (n : Nat) : isEven (n + 1) = ! isEven n := by
1147removed induction n with
1148removed | zero =>
1149removed rewrite [Nat.zero_add, isEven_zero, isEven_one]
1150removed rfl
1151removed | succ n ih =>
1152removed rewrite [isEven_succ_succ, ih, Bool.not_not]
1153removed rfl
1154removed
1155removed-- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims
1156removed-- in Lean: with booleans (of type `Bool`), and with
1157removed-- propositions (of type `Prop`).
1158removed
1159removed-- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1160removed
1161removed-- - ⠀
1162removed-- - `Bool`
1163removed-- - `Prop`
1164removed-- - decidable?
1165removed-- - yes
1166removed-- - no
1167removed-- - useable with `match`?
1168removed-- - yes
1169removed-- - no
1170removed-- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1171removed-- - no
1172removed-- - yes
1173removed
1174removed-- The crucial difference between the two worlds is
1175removed-- decidability. Every (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool`
1176removed-- can be simplified in a finite number of steps to either
1177removed-- `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating mechanical
1178removed-- procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1179removed
1180removed-- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is
1181removed-- inhabited only by functions that, given a `Nat`, always
1182removed-- yield either `true` or `false` in finite time; and this, in
1183removed-- turn, means (by a standard computability argument) that
1184removed-- there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1185removed-- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1186removed
1187removed-- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and
1188removed-- undecidable mathematical propositions; in particular, the
1189removed-- type `Nat → Prop` does contain functions representing
1190removed-- properties like "the nth Turing machine halts." The second
1191removed-- row in the table follows directly from this essential
1192removed-- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on
1193removed-- a boolean, we need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates
1194removed-- to `true` or `false`; this only works for `Bool`, not
1195removed-- `Prop`.
1196removed
1197removed-- The third row highlights an important practical difference:
1198removed-- equality functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean
1199removed-- cannot be used directly to justify rewriting with the
1200removed-- rewrite tactic; propositional equality is required for this.
1201removed-- Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1202removed-- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a
1203removed-- property that happens to be decidable: we can express it
1204removed-- either as a boolean computation or as a function into Prop.
1205removed
1206removed-- As an example, we can write
1207removed
1208removedunseal isEven in
1209removedexample : isEven 42 := rfl
1210removed
1211removed-- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1212removed
1213removedunseal double in
1214removedexample : Even 42 := by exists 21
1215removed
1216removed-- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two
1217removed-- characterizations of evenness did not describe the same set
1218removed-- of natural numbers!
1219removed
1220removed-- Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two
1221removed-- helper lemmas.
1222removed
1223removedtheorem even_double (k : Nat) : isEven (double k) = true := by
1224removed induction k with
1225removed | zero =>
1226removed rewrite [double_zero, isEven_zero]
1227removed rfl
1228removed | succ n ih =>
1229removed rewrite [double_succ, isEven_succ_succ]
1230removed exact ih
1231removed
1232removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): isEven_double_exists ⭐⭐⭐
1233removed
1234removedtheorem isEven_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1235removed ∃ k, n = bif isEven n then double k else double k + 1 := by sorry
1236removed
1237removed-- Now the main theorem:
1238removed
1239removedtheorem isEven_iff_Even {n : Nat} : isEven n = true ↔ Even n where
1240removed mp h := by
1241removed have ⟨k, hk⟩ := isEven_double_exists n
1242removed rewrite [h, cond_true] at hk
1243removed subst hk
1244removed exists k
1245removed mpr h := by
1246removed obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
1247removed subst hk
1248removed exact even_double k
1249removed
1250removed-- In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean
1251removed-- computation `isEven n` is reflected in the truth of the
1252removed-- proposition `∃ k, n = double k`.
1253removed
1254removed-- Similarly, to state that two numbers n and m are equal, we
1255removed-- can say either
1256removed
1257removed-- - that `n == m` returns `true`, or
1258removed-- - that `n = m`
1259removed
1260removed-- Again, these two notions are equivalent:
1261removed
1262removed-- Note to developers:
1263removed-- This proof is from the typeclass version, which makes
1264removed-- more sense if maps are included — CGH
1265removed
1266removedexample (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : n₁ == n₂ ↔ n₁ = n₂ := beq_iff_eq
1267removed
1268removed-- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be
1269removed-- formalized as either a proposition or a boolean computation?
1270removed-- Which should we choose?
1271removed
1272removed-- In general, both can be useful. Which we choose has to do
1273removed-- with the *computational* nature of Lean's core language,
1274removed-- which is designed so that every function it expresses is
1275removed-- total, and by default computable unless we explicit indicate
1276removed-- otherwise. As an example, consider trying to write a
1277removed-- function `α → α → Bool` checking for equality on an
1278removed-- arbitrary type:
1279removed

1308removed--
1309removed-- `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1310removed--
1311removed-- `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1312removed--
1313removed-- `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1314removed
1315removed-- Lean will complain here that it cannot find an instance of
1316removed-- `Decidable`. This typeclass
1317removed
1318removed-- Note to developers:
1319removed-- @dsainati - commenting this out because the -keep
1320removed-- doesn't work during extraction; this causes Lean to get
1321removed-- the two instances (the real one and this one) confused
1322removed--
1323removed-- `class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1324removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
1325removed-- | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1326removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1327removed-- | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p`
1328removed--
1329removed-- `class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1330removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
1331removed-- | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1332removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1333removed-- | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p`
1334removed--
1335removed-- `class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1336removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
1337removed-- | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1338removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1339removed-- | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p`
1340removed
1341removed-- is the way that we express in Lean that a given proposition
1342removed-- is decidable. This is the generalization of our observation
1343removed-- that `isEven_iff_Even` was reflecting a proof between
1344removed-- boolean and propositional equality. In fact, we can use this
1345removed-- theorem to directly construct a `Decidable` instance
1346removed
1347removedinstance (n : Nat) : Decidable (Even n) := decidable_of_decidable_of_iff isEven_iff_Even
1348removed
1349removed-- Now we are able to complete such proofs by computation using
1350removed-- the `decide` tactic:
1351removed
1352removedsection
1353removedunseal isEven
1354removed
1355removedexample : Even 2 := by decide
1356removedexample : Even 4 := by decide
1357removedexample : Even 6 := by decide
1358removedexample : Even 100 := by decide
1359removedexample : ¬ Even 101 := by decide
1360removedexample : ∀ n < 10, Even (2 * n) := by decide
1361removedexample : ∀ n < 10, Even (2 * n) ∧ ¬ Even (2 * n + 1) := by decide
1362removedend
1363removed
1364removed-- In general, Lean will try to use typeclass synthesis with
1365removed-- `Decidable` in order to determine when it is appropriate to
1366removed-- use `Prop` and `Bool` interchangeably. For instance, while
1367removed-- our example `eq` failed above while trying to use
1368removed-- propositional equality `=` in the condition of an `if`
1369removed-- statement, we are allowed to write
1370removed
1371removeddef nat_eq (m n : Nat) : Bool := if m = n then true else false
1372removed
1373removed-- Why is this allowed? It is precisely because equality of
1374removed-- natural numbers is decidable, and Lean makes use of this
1375removed-- fact. If we print this definition with notation unset, we
1376removed-- would find that it is using `instDecidableEqNat`
1377removed
1378removedset_option pp.all true in
1379removed#print nat_eq
1380removed
1381removed-- which proves that this equality is decidable.
1382removed
1383removed-- This is only half the story however: while Lean's core
1384removed-- theory enables this computation, Lean is also often used in
1385removed-- applications where we don't care about computability, such
1386removed-- as pure mathematics. In particular, it is possible to write
1387removed-- a function for arbitrary equality:
1388removed
1389removedsf_experiment
1390removed open scoped Classical in
1391removed noncomputable def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false
1392removed
1393removed set_option pp.all true in
1394removed #print eq
1395removed
1396removed-- But we have indicated to Lean, using the `noncomputable`
1397removed-- keyword and `Classical` namespace that we are *not*
1398removed-- interested in computation. What is happening in the
1399removed-- background is that this allows typeclass synthesis to find
1400removed-- the scoped instance `Classical.propDecidable`, which makes
1401removed-- use of the axiom of choice to provide a proof that all
1402removed-- propositions are *classically* decidable. This sort of
1403removed-- definition is suitable for use with proofs, but is not
1404removed-- allowed to be used in conjunction with computational
1405removed-- features of Lean such as the `decide` tactic or the `#eval`
1406removed-- command.
